'''Charles Alfred Taylor''' (14 August 1922 &ndash; 7 March 2002) was a British [[physicist]], known for his work in [[crystallography]] and his efforts to promote science to young audiences.

==Early life and education==
Charles Taylor was born in [[Kingston upon Hull|Hull]] in 1922.<ref name=indy-orb>{{cite news |url= https://www.independent.co.uk/news/obituaries/professor-charles-taylor-729852.html |title= Obituary: Professor Charles Taylor |work= The Independent |archiveurl= https://web.archive.org/web/20110111184109/http://www.independent.co.uk/news/obituaries/professor-charles-taylor-729852.html |archivedate= 2011-01-11 |url-status=dead |date= 23 March 2002 |accessdate= 4 April 2011}}</ref> He began his degree at [[Queen Mary College]] (a constituent college of the [[University of London]]), but the college was subsequently evacuated to [[Cambridge]] during World War II. He graduated in 1943 and after working for the Admiralty during the war, worked as a lecturer and then a reader after completing his PhD.

==Career==
Taylor's first work was for the [[British Admiralty|Admiralty]], designing [[radar]] [[countermeasures]], work that eventually took him to [[Harvard]] University in the United States until the end of the war. He then studied for a [[PhD]] at the [[University of Manchester Institute of Science and Technology]], and continued there from 1948 until 1965. He worked for a long time with [[Henry Lipson]] on the development of optical diffraction analogue methods. He was awarded a [[DSc]] in 1960.

In 1965 he moved with his family to [[Cardiff]] to take up the position of Chair of Physics at [[Cardiff University|University College Cardiff]], where the main interest of the department was [[X-ray crystallography]], in the same field as the work he did with Lipson in Manchester.

He was appointed to the post of Visiting Professor of Experimental Physics at the [[Royal Institution]], a post he held until 1988. He also gave many lectures to schoolchildren. In 1990, he lectured to thousands of children in Tokyo as a follow-up to his Christmas Lectures in London the previous year.{{cn|date=December 2024}}

==Publications==
Taylor was the author of a number of books, including ''The Art and Science of Lecture Demonstration''. He co-wrote, with Stephen Pople, the worldwide-selling ''Oxford Children's Book of Science'' (1994).

==Lectures==
As well as his work in research, Taylor had close links to the [[Royal Institution]].  He had always had a strong interest in music and its relationship with physics.  In 1971, he lectured to schoolchildren for the [[Royal Institution Christmas Lectures]] on ''The Sounds of Music'', covering physics and music. In 1989 he became the third person since 1945 to deliver a second series of Christmas lectures, ''Exploring Music''.<ref name="indy-orb" />

==Honours==
Taylor was awarded the [[Institute_of_Physics_Awards#The_Lawrence_Bragg_Medal_and_Prize|Lawrence Bragg Medal]] by the [[Institute of Physics]] in 1983 for his outstanding and sustained contributions to physics education.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.iop.org/about/awards/gold-medals/lawrence-bragg-medal-and-prize-recipients#gref|title=''Lawrence Bragg Medal and Prize recipients''|website=Institute of Physics|access-date=9 February 2021}}</ref> In 1986 he was unanimously awarded the first [[Michael Faraday Award]] by the [[Royal Society]] for communicating science to public audiences.  Altogether, he gave over 150 lectures to schoolchildren at the Royal Institution, as well as presenting eight Friday evening discourses there.{{cn|date=December 2024}}

==Personal life==
Taylor married Nancy Truefitt in 1942. They had three children.<ref name="indy-orb" /> He died at Warminster, Wiltshire on 7 March 2002.<ref name="indy-orb" />
